posts.title: Creepy Tale: Snow Child Review #Keymailer
posts.description: Those who know me, or read my reviews regularly, are aware of the fact that I’m a big fan of horror. I also appreciate unique takes within the genre, across various mediums. As such, lots of interesting releases pique my interest, and sometimes take me out of my comfort zone. That was the case with Creepy Tale: Snow Child , which is apparently the fifth game in a series that I was new to upon starting it. This particular release takes the form of a stylized story/puzzle game with character movement and dialogue, and one that isn’t exactly typical fare for the genre. Being that I’ve always struggled with, and often avoided, puzzle games, it took me out of my comfort zone. When I’d requested it, I’d seen the art style, read the premise and saw that it had puzzles, but I didn’t expect them to be so prevalent or unique, or (sometimes) obtuse. posts.title: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time [2026] Review
posts.description: Some games age like fine red wine potion, while some age like Lon Lon Milk left outside the castle in the July sun. The original The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time has always been a bit of both, but we’ve looked past its flaws for decades with rose-coloured glasses. Look, I’ve got a Triforce tattoo on my wrist, so I’m certainly no Zelda hater. The original Ocarina of Time is an absolute masterpiece and is, beyond a Shadow Temple of a doubt, one of my favourite games of all time. But reviewing its remake means being honest and as unbiased as possible. The original game’s ideas are timeless, while its murky fog, stubborn camera and that infamous Water Temple menu shuffle have been showing their wrinkles for a while now. So, for the series’ 40th anniversary, Nintendo set out to answer a simple question: what happens if you keep the potion and toss the milk? posts.title: Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 [Switch 2] Review
posts.description: Modern Warfare 4 on Switch 2 is a full, complete Call of Duty you can carry in a bag, and that alone makes it worth talking about. It is also, perhaps obviously, the roughest-looking version of the game you can buy. Whether that trade-off makes sense depends almost entirely on which other consoles, if any, sit under your TV. And, whether you want to take this game on the go. The last Call of Duty on a Nintendo console was Ghosts on the Wii U in 2013. Modern Warfare 4 ends that 13-year gap day and date with the PS5, Xbox Series, and PC, as Infinity Ward, with the help of Digital Legends, brings its latest adventure to Nintendo’s latest console. The campaign, multiplayer, DMZ, crossplay and cross-progression are all here. The real question is what the hardware gives up to fit it all into that 131 GB download.
